paragraphs.source_en: Today the collieries that fuelled the Industrial Revolution in Britain have virtually all closed, as remaining coal seams became ever more difficult to access, cheaper coal became available overseas, and less polluting or renewable energy sources were sought. ¶ A few opencast mines remain, but the last of the deep mines in the UK, Kellingley in Yorkshire, closed in 2015. 27 Yet astonishingly, the distribution of the 320-million-year-old coalfields in the UK still leaves its imprint on Britain's political map today.

paragraphs.source_en: The Labour Party was founded in 1900 from the trade union movement, with particularly close ties to British coal miners. And although it has changed a great deal over the last hundred years–from a party in the shadow of the Liberals to a landslide victory just after the Second World War to New Labour under Tony Blair–the deep link between coal and politics has endured for generations. Take the results of the most recent General Election, in 2017, for example, shown on here. The election was much closer than the map would seem to imply, with densely populated, multicultural cities such as London tending to lean to Labour and the sparsely populated, larger, rural constituencies overwhelmingly voting Conservative. The result was a hung parliament with Labour winning 262 seats in parliament and the Conservatives 318–not enough for a majority government.

paragraphs.source_en: But let's look more closely at the distribution of Labour votes across the country. The figure here shows the location of Britain's coalfields, and what is remarkable is the tight correlation between the political and geological maps. The broad coalfields of Cumberland, Northumberland and Durham (the Great Northern), Lancashire, Yorkshire, Staffordshire, North and South Wales, all match perfectly with the large areas of Labour constituencies in the election. This correlation was even stronger in the 2015 election, when Labour's crushing defeat confined it to its heartlands, and the pattern is evident throughout the previous decades. Support for the main leftwing political party in the UK almost perfectly matches the regions of Carboniferous deposits. * It seems that the old geology deep underground is still reflected in people's lives today.
